questions.question: Which data structure is defined as a collection of similar data elements?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Array.**

An array is a contiguous collection of elements of the same type indexed by position.

questions.question: Which among the following is a LIFO data structure?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) Stack.**

The last element pushed is the first one popped. A queue is FIFO.

questions.question: Which data structure is used to represent complex relationships between the nodes?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) Graph.**

Graphs model arbitrary many-to-many relationships; trees are restricted acyclic hierarchies.

questions.question: Typical time requirement for operation on queues is —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) O(1).**

With head/tail pointers, enqueue and dequeue are constant-time operations.

questions.question: The depth of root node is —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) 0.**

Using the common level/depth convention, the root is at depth 0. Some books number levels from 1, but the printed options and marked answer use 0.

questions.question: A binary tree of height h has at least h nodes and at most —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) 2^h − 1 nodes.**

A full binary tree of height h has `1 + 2 + ... + 2^(h-1) = 2^h − 1` nodes when height counts levels.
questions.sourceNote: OCR flattened exponents to `2h`, `2h`, `2h+1`, `2h-1`; restored from the page image as powers of 2.

questions.question: When the left sub-tree of the tree is one level higher than that of the right sub-tree, then the balance factor is —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) 1.**

With balance factor = height(left) − height(right), a left-heavy difference of one level gives +1.

questions.question: Total number of nodes at the nth level of a binary tree can be given as —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) 2^(n-1).**

If the root is level 1, level n has at most `2^(n-1)` nodes.
questions.sourceNote: Exponents were visually confirmed from the page crop; option D is `2^(n-1)`.

questions.question: Which type of linked list can have four pointers per node?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) multi-linked list.**

A multi-linked node may hold several links, e.g. next, previous, child, and parent.

questions.question: A graph in which there exists a path between two of its nodes is called —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) connected graph.**

A connected graph has a path between every pair of vertices. A complete graph additionally has an edge between every pair.

questions.question: The total number of edges containing the node u is called —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) degree.**

Degree counts all incident edges; in-degree/out-degree apply to directed graphs.

questions.question: Which type of linked list does not store NULL in the next field?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) circular linked list.**

The last node points back to the first, so the chain has no NULL next pointer.

questions.question: The circular queue will be full only when —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) front = 0 and rear = max − 1.**

In the simple array implementation shown, the queue is full when the rear reaches the last slot and the front is at the first slot.
questions.sourceNote: OCR merged option B across a line break; restored from the page crop.

questions.question: Reverse Polish Notation is the other name of —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) postfix expression.**

In postfix / Reverse Polish Notation, operators follow their operands.

questions.question: Linked list is used to implement data structures like —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) all of these.**

Linked nodes can implement stacks, queues, and tree/graph adjacency structures.

questions.question:
a) What do you understand by stack overflow and stack underflow?
b) Differentiate between an array and a stack.
c) Write algorithms for PUSH and POP.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: What do you understand by stack overflow and stack underflow?

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Differentiate between an array and a stack.

subparts.label: c
subparts.text: Write algorithms for PUSH and POP.

questions.answer:
**a)** Overflow occurs when pushing onto a full stack; underflow occurs when popping from an empty stack.

**b)** An array is random-access by index; a stack is an ADT restricted to push/pop at one end.

**c)**
```text
PUSH(S, x): if top == MAX-1 overflow; else S[++top] = x
POP(S):     if top == -1 underflow; else return S[top--]
```
questions.sourceNote: The scan prints the split as `2+2+(2+2)`; PUSH and POP are combined into one 4-mark subpart here.

questions.question:
a) What is a priority queue? Give its applications.
b) Explain the concept of a circular queue. How is it better than a linear queue?

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: What is a priority queue? Give its applications.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Explain the concept of a circular queue. How is it better than a linear queue?

questions.answer:
**a)** A priority queue removes the element with highest priority first. Uses: CPU scheduling, Dijkstra’s algorithm, Huffman coding, print spoolers.

**b)** A circular queue wraps the rear to the front using modulo arithmetic, reusing freed slots. A linear array queue can appear full even when earlier slots are empty after dequeues.

questions.question:
a) Make a comparison between a linked list and a linear array.
b) Which one will you prefer to use and when?
c) Why is a doubly linked list more useful than a singly linked list?
d) Give the advantages and uses of a circular linked list.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Make a comparison between a linked list and a linear array.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Which one will you prefer to use and when?

subparts.label: c
subparts.text: Why is a doubly linked list more useful than a singly linked list?

subparts.label: d
subparts.text: Give the advantages and uses of a circular linked list.

questions.answer:
**a)** Arrays give O(1) indexed access but fixed size; linked lists give O(1) insertion/deletion with a known pointer but O(n) search.

**b)** Prefer arrays for frequent random access; linked lists for frequent insertions/deletions.

**c)** Doubly linked lists allow backward traversal and O(1) deletion when the node is known.

**d)** Circular lists support round-robin traversal and queues; any node can reach all others without a NULL terminator.

questions.question:
a) Differentiate between an iterative function and a recursive function. Which one will you prefer to use and in what circumstances?
b) Convert the expression given below into its corresponding postfix expression and then evaluate it: `10 + -((7 - 5) + 10) / 2`.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Differentiate between an iterative function and a recursive function. Which one will you prefer to use and in what circumstances?

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Convert the expression given below into its corresponding postfix expression and then evaluate it: `10 + -((7 - 5) + 10) / 2`.

questions.answer:
**a)** Iteration uses loops and explicit state; recursion calls itself and uses the call stack. Prefer iteration for simple repetition and tight memory; recursion for tree/graph traversal and divide-and-conquer.

**b)** Treating the minus before the bracket as unary negation:

Postfix: `10 7 5 - 10 + NEG 2 / +`

Evaluation: `(7-5)+10 = 12`; `-12/2 = -6`; `10 + (-6) = 4`.
questions.sourceNote: The scan prints `(2+1+1)+(2+2)` and the expression with scan ink over the unary minus; restored as `10 + -((7 - 5) + 10) / 2`.

questions.question:
a) Specify the use of a header node in a header linked list.
b) Give the linked representation of the polynomial `7x³y² − 8x²y + 3xy + 11x + 4`.
c) Explain the difference between a circular linked list and a singly linked list.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Specify the use of a header node in a header linked list.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Give the linked representation of the polynomial `7x³y² − 8x²y + 3xy + 11x + 4`.

subparts.label: c
subparts.text: Explain the difference between a circular linked list and a singly linked list.

questions.answer:
**a)** A header/dummy node simplifies insertion, deletion, and empty-list handling because the first real node always has a predecessor.

**b)** Each node stores coefficient and exponents, linked in descending order:

```text
(7,3,2) -> (-8,2,1) -> (3,1,1) -> (11,1,0) -> (4,0,0) -> NULL
```

**c)** A singly list ends in NULL; a circular list links the last node back to the first/header.
questions.sourceNote: The polynomial was visually confirmed from a 10× crop: `7x³y² − 8x²y + 3xy + 11x + 4`.

questions.question:
a) What are the two ways of representing binary trees in the memory? Which one do you prefer and why?
b) List all possible non-similar binary trees having four nodes.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: What are the two ways of representing binary trees in the memory? Which one do you prefer and why?

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: List all possible non-similar binary trees having four nodes.

questions.answer:
**a)** Array/sequential representation and linked/node representation. Linked representation is usually preferred because it handles arbitrary shapes without wasting array slots.

**b)** The number of non-similar binary trees with 4 nodes is the Catalan number `C₄ = 14`. They are all distinct shapes obtained by choosing left-subtree sizes 0..3 and combining the corresponding smaller trees.

questions.answer:
```text
start: []
```

questions.question:
a) How are graphs represented inside a computer’s memory? Which method do you prefer and why?
b) Draw a complete undirected graph having five nodes.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: How are graphs represented inside a computer’s memory? Which method do you prefer and why?

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Draw a complete undirected graph having five nodes.

questions.answer:
**a)** Common representations: adjacency matrix and adjacency list. Lists are preferred for sparse graphs because they use O(V+E) space; matrices give O(1) edge lookup and suit dense graphs.

**b)** `K₅` has five vertices with every pair connected, so it has `5×4/2 = 10` undirected edges. A pentagon plus all five diagonals is one drawing.
